lessons.title: Interactions that change what you see
lessons.body:
Most drug interactions are a pharmacist's problem. A handful are yours, because they change the findings in front of you or the treatment you are about to give.

## The masks

**Beta blockers hide two emergencies.** Blocking beta-1 means the heart cannot speed up, so a bleeding or septic patient stays at `70` beats per minute while dying. Blocking beta-2 also removes the tremor and pounding heart of hypoglycemia, so a diabetic on metoprolol may go from normal to unconscious with only sweating as a warning. Sweating is driven by a different nerve pathway and survives the block.

> **Key:** On a beta blocker, judge perfusion by skin, mental status and capillary refill, and check a glucose on anyone who seems off. The heart rate is not a witness you can trust.

**Anticoagulants hide time.** Warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban and clopidogrel do not cause bleeding; they prevent it from stopping. A minor head strike becomes a bleed that may declare itself `6 to 72 hours` later, which is why the patient with a normal exam still goes in. Two things make it worse: an added NSAID such as ibuprofen or naproxen, which attacks the stomach lining at the same time, and antibiotics like trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, ciprofloxacin or metronidazole, which push a warfarin patient's clotting time higher within days.

**Insulin hides a missed meal.** Long-acting insulin such as glargine is dosed for a normal eating day. Skip dinner, add a stomach bug, work a double shift, or start a new exercise routine, and the insulin keeps working with nothing to work on. The classic call is hypoglycemia at `0300` in a patient who felt fine at bedtime.

## The amplifiers

**MAO inhibitors and stimulants.** Phenelzine (Nardil), tranylcypromine (Parnate) and selegiline block the enzyme that clears norepinephrine. Add a sympathomimetic — pseudoephedrine, an amphetamine, cocaine, even aged cheese and cured meats — and the surge has nowhere to go. The result is a hypertensive crisis: a sudden severe headache, a systolic over `200`, chest pain, and possible stroke. These drugs are uncommon now, which is exactly why they show up on exams.

**Serotonin syndrome.** An SSRI such as sertraline plus tramadol, linezolid, dextromethorphan, a triptan or MDMA floods serotonin receptors. Look for the triad: agitation or confusion, overactive reflexes and clonus (rhythmic jerking, most obvious at the ankles), and autonomic instability with fever, sweating, diarrhea and tachycardia. It comes on over `hours`. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome, its lookalike, comes from antipsychotics, builds over `days`, and produces lead-pipe rigidity with slowed reflexes instead of clonus.

**Diuretics and digoxin.** Furosemide and hydrochlorothiazide dump potassium. Low potassium makes the heart more sensitive to digoxin, so a stable dose becomes a toxic one: nausea, vomiting, confusion, yellow-green halos around lights, and slow or irregular rhythms.

**ACE inhibitors and the tongue.** Lisinopril and its relatives cause angioedema — swelling of the lips, tongue and throat with **no hives and no itching** — and it can start years into treatment. It is not an allergic reaction driven by histamine, so epinephrine and antihistamines often do little. Give epinephrine anyway if the airway is closing, because you cannot rule out anaphylaxis in the field, but the real treatment is an airway and a hospital.

**Depressants stack.** Alcohol plus a benzodiazepine plus an opioid depresses breathing more than the sum of the parts. Naloxone reverses only the opioid piece, so a partial response does not mean you missed the dose.

> **On shift:** Two questions surface most of this at the bedside: what changed in the last two weeks, and what did you take today that you do not take every day.
keyPoints: Beta blockers mask both the tachycardia of shock and the tremor and palpitations of hypoglycemia; sweating still occurs.
Anticoagulants plus a head strike means a delayed bleed; NSAIDs and certain antibiotics amplify the bleeding risk.
Long-acting insulin with a missed meal or illness produces hypoglycemia hours later, classically overnight.
MAO inhibitors plus a sympathomimetic cause hypertensive crisis; SSRIs plus tramadol or linezolid cause serotonin syndrome with clonus and fever.
ACE inhibitor angioedema swells the lips and tongue without hives or itching and responds poorly to epinephrine, though you still give it for a threatened airway.

checks.q: A 62-year-old on carvedilol has been vomiting blood. Skin is cool and mottled, capillary refill is 4 seconds, HR 72, BP 96/58. How do you interpret the heart rate?
choices: He is compensating well because the rate is normal
The beta blocker prevents the expected tachycardia, so judge perfusion by skin, mental status and refill
The heart rate rules out significant blood loss
The rate means he is bradycardic and needs pacing
checks.why: Beta-1 blockade prevents the heart from speeding up in response to blood loss, so the number is uninformative. Skin signs and capillary refill say he is in shock now.

checks.q: A patient on sertraline started tramadol two days ago. He is agitated and sweating, with a temperature of 101.8 F, a heart rate of 124, and rhythmic jerking of the ankles when you flex the feet. What is this?
choices: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Alcohol withdrawal
Serotonin syndrome
A simple febrile illness
checks.why: Agitation, clonus and autonomic instability developing over hours after adding a serotonergic drug is serotonin syndrome. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows antipsychotics, develops over days, and causes rigidity with slowed reflexes.

checks.q: A 70-year-old on lisinopril has a swollen tongue and lips with no hives and no itching. What is true?
choices: This is histamine-driven and will resolve quickly with epinephrine alone
It cannot be caused by a medication he has taken for years
Antihistamines are the definitive treatment
It is ACE inhibitor angioedema, which responds poorly to epinephrine, though epinephrine is still given for a threatened airway
checks.why: ACE inhibitor angioedema is not histamine-mediated, so the usual allergy drugs underperform, and it can begin years into therapy. You still give epinephrine for airway compromise because you cannot exclude anaphylaxis in the field.

lessons.title: Reverse-engineering the patient from the pill bottles
lessons.body:
One drug names a problem. A combination names a patient. Before the family finishes answering your history questions, the counter has already told you what this person lives with, how sick they are, and what is most likely going wrong today.

## Combinations that describe a disease

| What you see | What it means | What to expect today |
|---|---|---|
| Metoprolol, furosemide, lisinopril, spironolactone | Heart failure with reduced pumping | Fluid overload, orthopnea, weight gain, a blunted heart rate |
| Apixaban, diltiazem, digoxin | Atrial fibrillation | Irregular pulse, bleeding risk, digoxin toxicity if potassium is low |
| Tiotropium, albuterol refilled monthly, a prednisone taper, home oxygen | Severe COPD | Titrate oxygen to `88 to 92%`, expect a high baseline carbon dioxide |
| Insulin pump plus a continuous glucose sensor | Type 1 diabetes | Both hypoglycemia and a fast slide into ketoacidosis |
| Methotrexate, adalimumab, prednisone | Immune system suppressed on purpose | A fever is an emergency; infection can look mild until it is not |
| Ondansetron, oxycodone, a port in the chest | Active cancer treatment | Neutropenic fever, dehydration, pain crises |
| Hydroxyurea, folic acid, oxycodone | Sickle cell disease | Pain crisis, chest syndrome, believe the reported pain |
| Carbidopa-levodopa dosed five times a day | Parkinson's disease | Missed doses cause rigidity, falls and swallowing failure |
| Buprenorphine-naloxone or methadone | Opioid use disorder in treatment | High tolerance, and naloxone works poorly against buprenorphine |

## Single bottles that change the call

**Daily prednisone for months** means the adrenal glands have stopped making their own stress hormone. An infection, injury or vomiting illness can drop this patient into adrenal crisis: weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain and hypotension that does not respond to position. They need hospital steroids, and your job is recognizing it and saying it.

**Clozapine** can wipe out white blood cells, so any fever in a clozapine patient is a genuine emergency rather than a nuisance.

**Lithium** has almost no margin between working and toxic. Dehydration, a new NSAID or a new ACE inhibitor pushes it over: coarse tremor, vomiting, unsteady walking and confusion.

**Levothyroxine** marks a thyroid that does not work. **Allopurinol** marks gout. **Tamsulosin** marks prostate symptoms and a standing blood pressure that drops. **Donepezil** marks dementia, which sets a baseline you must ask the family to describe.

> **Trap:** Revatio and Adcirca are sildenafil and tadalafil prescribed for pulmonary hypertension. A `74-year-old` woman on Revatio absolutely has a nitroglycerin contraindication, and nobody will volunteer it if you ask about erectile dysfunction drugs.

## Reading the label, not just the name

The non-drug information on a bottle is often the most useful part.

- **Fill date and count.** Thirty tablets filled `40 days` ago with `25` left means the patient is not taking them. That single observation explains a huge number of hypertensive, seizure and psychiatric calls.
- **Prescriber.** Four different prescribers on four bottles means nobody is coordinating.
- **A brand-new bottle.** Anything started in the last `2 weeks` is a suspect for today's problem.
- **What is missing.** A diabetic with no glucometer, an asthmatic with no rescue inhaler, a heart failure patient who ran out of furosemide: absence is history too.

> **On shift:** Photograph the labels or bag the bottles and bring them. Then say the three findings out loud in your report: what the combination suggests, what is new, and what has not been taken.
keyPoints: A combination of drugs names a disease; read the counter as a problem list before you finish the history.
Chronic daily prednisone means adrenal suppression and possible adrenal crisis during illness or injury.
Revatio and Adcirca are PDE-5 inhibitors for pulmonary hypertension and contraindicate nitroglycerin regardless of the patient's age or sex.
Fill date, tablet count, prescriber and recent starts tell you about adherence and about today's cause.
Missing medications and missing equipment are findings worth reporting.

checks.q: A patient's counter holds metoprolol, furosemide, lisinopril and spironolactone. What does this combination most suggest?
choices: Heart failure, so expect fluid overload and a heart rate that will not rise
Asthma with frequent exacerbations
Type 2 diabetes
Chronic kidney disease only
checks.why: That set is the standard treatment for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Anticipate orthopnea and fluid overload, and remember the beta blocker will blunt any tachycardia.

checks.q: You find a bottle of 30 levetiracetam tablets filled 40 days ago with 25 tablets remaining in a patient who just had a seizure. What does this tell you?
choices: The medication is working well
He has been taking roughly one dose every eight days, so missed doses are the likely seizure trigger
The bottle was recently refilled and is irrelevant
He needs a higher dose
checks.why: Five tablets used in forty days is near-total nonadherence, and missed antiepileptic doses are among the most common seizure triggers. Report the count, not just the drug name.

lessons.title: Twenty medication math cases, worked
lessons.body:
Three formulas cover almost everything an EMT calculates. Pounds divided by `2.2` is kilograms. Volume equals the dose you want divided by the concentration on the label. A percent solution is grams per `100 mL`. Work these until the arithmetic disappears and only the checking remains.

## Weight

1. A man weighs `154 lb`. `154` divided by `2.2` equals `70 kg`.
2. A child weighs `33 lb`. `33` divided by `2.2` equals `15 kg` — the bottom of the pediatric auto-injector band.
3. A teenager weighs `132 lb`. `132` divided by `2.2` equals `60 kg`, so adult dosing applies.
4. Fast estimate for `190 lb`: half is `95`, minus `10%` is about `85 kg`. The exact answer is `86.4 kg`, close enough to sanity-check a dose.
5. A child's weight is unknown. Measure heel to head with a length-based tape and read the color band, which gives weight and doses together.

## Volume from a concentration

6. Epinephrine `1 mg/mL`, adult anaphylaxis dose `0.3 mg`: `0.3` divided by `1` equals `0.3 mL`.
7. Epinephrine `1 mg/mL`, pediatric dose `0.15 mg`: `0.15` divided by `1` equals `0.15 mL`.
8. Epinephrine `0.1 mg/mL` (the cardiac arrest concentration), `0.3 mg` wanted: `0.3` divided by `0.1` equals `3 mL`. Ten times the volume for the same dose — and the wrong vial for an IM injection.
9. Weight-based pediatric epinephrine at `0.01 mg/kg` for a `12 kg` child: `0.12 mg`. From `1 mg/mL`, that is `0.12 mL`.
10. Naloxone `1 mg/mL`, `2 mg` wanted IM: `2` divided by `1` equals `2 mL`.
11. Naloxone `0.4 mg/mL`, `0.4 mg` wanted: `1 mL`.
12. Intranasal naloxone `2 mg` in `2 mL` total, split between nostrils: `1 mL` and `1 mg` per side.

## Tablets, sprays and unit doses

13. Aspirin `324 mg` from `81 mg` chewables: `324` divided by `81` equals `4` tablets, chewed.
14. Nitroglycerin `0.4 mg` per dose, maximum `3` doses: `1.2 mg` total, with a blood pressure check before each one.
15. Albuterol comes as a `2.5 mg` unit-dose vial in `3 mL`. You give the whole vial; there is nothing to calculate.

## Percent solutions and grams

16. `D50` means `50 g` per `100 mL`, which is `0.5 g/mL`. A `50 mL` prefilled syringe therefore contains `25 g` of dextrose.
17. `D10` means `10 g` per `100 mL`, or `0.1 g/mL`. To deliver the same `25 g` takes `250 mL`.
18. Normal saline is `0.9%`, meaning `0.9 g` per `100 mL`, so a `1,000 mL` bag holds `9 g` of sodium chloride.
19. Activated charcoal at `1 g/kg` for an `80 kg` adult calculates to `80 g`, but the usual adult dose is capped at `25 to 50 g` per protocol. Calculate it, then check it against the protocol range.

## Oxygen supply

20. Remaining minutes equal pressure minus a `200 psi` safe residual, times the cylinder constant, divided by the flow rate. For a `D` cylinder the constant is `0.16`, for an `E` cylinder `0.28`, and for an `M` cylinder `1.56`. An `E` cylinder reading `1,800 psi` running at `15 L/min`: `1,800` minus `200` is `1,600`; `1,600` times `0.28` is `448`; `448` divided by `15` is about `30 minutes`.

> **Key:** Every calculation gets said out loud to your partner before it goes into a patient: drug, concentration, dose, volume. The error you catch is the one you spoke.

> **Trap:** The decimal point is the most dangerous character in medicine. `0.15 mg` and `1.5 mg` are one keystroke apart, and a leading zero (`0.3`, never `.3`) is what keeps a dose from being read as ten times too large.
keyPoints: Pounds divided by 2.2 is kilograms; halve and subtract 10 percent for a field estimate.
Volume to give equals the desired dose divided by the label concentration.
Epinephrine 1 mg/mL is the IM anaphylaxis concentration; 0.1 mg/mL requires ten times the volume for the same dose.
A percent solution is grams per 100 mL, so D50 is 0.5 g/mL and a 50 mL syringe holds 25 g.
Oxygen minutes remaining equal pressure minus 200 psi, times the cylinder constant, divided by flow; the E cylinder constant is 0.28.

checks.q: You need 0.15 mg of epinephrine for a 20 kg child and the vial reads 1 mg/mL. What volume do you draw?
choices: 1.5 mL
0.5 mL
checks.why: 0.15 divided by 1 equals 0.15 mL. Note the decimal: 1.5 mL would be ten times the intended dose, which is exactly how this error happens.

checks.q: An E cylinder reads 1,400 psi and you are running 10 L/min. Approximately how long until you must switch tanks?
choices: About 15 minutes
About 22 minutes
About 34 minutes
About 50 minutes
checks.why: 1,400 minus the 200 psi safe residual is 1,200; times the E constant of 0.28 is 336; divided by 10 L/min is about 34 minutes. Always subtract the residual first.

checks.q: A 50 mL prefilled syringe is labeled D50. How many grams of dextrose does it contain?
choices: 5 g
checks.why: A percent solution is grams per 100 mL, so D50 is 0.5 g per mL. Fifty milliliters times 0.5 g/mL is 25 g.

lessons.title: Epinephrine in the hard cases
lessons.body:
The standard anaphylaxis call is easy: `0.3 mg` in the thigh and a fast ride. These are the versions that make people hesitate, and hesitating is the error.

## The beta-blocked patient

Epinephrine works by turning on alpha and beta receptors. A patient on metoprolol, atenolol or carvedilol has the beta receptors partially blocked, so the airway opening and the increase in cardiac output are blunted while the alpha-driven vasoconstriction is not. Two consequences follow: the reaction may not break after the first dose, and the blood pressure can rise sharply.

What you do is unchanged — give the epinephrine, repeat it at `5 to 15 minutes` if the reaction persists, request ALS early, and tell the receiving hospital about the beta blocker. The definitive answer for a beta-blocked patient who does not respond is **glucagon** `1 to 5 mg` intravenously, which raises cardiac output through a completely different receptor. Some systems authorize BLS glucagon for hypoglycemia only, so this is usually an ALS or hospital intervention.

> **Key:** A beta blocker never makes epinephrine the wrong drug. It only makes one dose more likely to be insufficient.

## The cardiac patient and the very old

Epinephrine raises heart rate and the heart's oxygen demand, and in a `78-year-old` with coronary disease that carries a genuine risk of chest pain or an arrhythmia. Compare the risks honestly: untreated anaphylaxis kills in minutes, and death from epinephrine given intramuscularly for anaphylaxis is vanishingly rare. Give the standard `0.3 mg` in the thigh, do not reduce the dose on your own, monitor closely, and expect the tachycardia.

The genuinely dangerous version is the wrong route or concentration. Almost every serious epinephrine injury comes from an intravenous push of a concentration meant for intramuscular use.

## Pediatric weight bands

| Weight | Device or dose |
|---|---|
| `7.5 to 15 kg` | `0.1 mg` auto-injector where available, or `0.01 mg/kg` drawn up |
| `15 to 30 kg` | `0.15 mg` pediatric auto-injector |
| `30 kg` and above | `0.3 mg` adult auto-injector |

By syringe the rule is `0.01 mg/kg` of the `1 mg/mL` concentration, to a maximum of `0.3 mg` in most protocols, up to `0.5 mg` in some. For an infant under `7.5 kg`, auto-injectors have needles that are too long and doses that are too large, so the drawn-up calculation is the only correct answer.

**Technique failures specific to children.** Hold the leg still: a struggling child plus a spring-loaded needle is how thigh lacerations happen. Use the outer middle third of the thigh, `90 degrees`, through clothing but not through a pocket with keys or a phone in it. Newer devices hold for `3 seconds`, older ones for `10` — read the device.

> **Trap:** Thumb over the wrong end. The needle fires from the tip, and an injection into a fingertip causes a white, cold, numb digit that needs an emergency department. If it happens, keep the hand warm, transport, and tell them the time.

## Other places epinephrine appears

**Severe asthma** that does not respond to nebulized albuterol is treated with IM epinephrine `0.3 mg` in some systems, on the same reasoning as anaphylaxis: beta-2 stimulation opens the airway. Varies by protocol.

**Anaphylaxis without hives.** About one in five reactions has no skin findings at all. Sudden vomiting and hypotension after a sting or a known food, or airway symptoms with an exposure, is anaphylaxis until proven otherwise. Waiting for a rash is a fatal habit.

**Biphasic reactions** return `4 to 12 hours` later, which is why every patient goes in, including the one who feels completely normal by the time you reach the truck.
keyPoints: Beta-blocked patients may not respond to one dose; repeat it, call ALS, and expect the hospital to add glucagon 1 to 5 mg IV.
Cardiac history and advanced age are cautions, not contraindications; give the standard 0.3 mg IM in the thigh.
Pediatric bands: 0.1 mg for 7.5 to 15 kg where available, 0.15 mg for 15 to 30 kg, 0.3 mg at 30 kg and above, or 0.01 mg/kg drawn up.
Hold a child's leg still, inject the outer middle third of the thigh at 90 degrees, and never put a thumb over the needle end.
About 20 percent of anaphylaxis has no hives, and biphasic reactions return 4 to 12 hours later, so everyone is transported.

checks.q: A 71-year-old on atenolol has anaphylaxis after a bee sting. Five minutes after 0.3 mg of epinephrine his stridor persists and his BP is 84/48. What is correct?
choices: Halve the next dose because of his age
Withhold further epinephrine because of the beta blocker
Repeat the epinephrine, request ALS, and tell the hospital he is on a beta blocker so glucagon can be considered
Give only oxygen and transport
checks.why: Beta blockade blunts the response, making a second dose more likely to be needed rather than less. Glucagon bypasses the blocked receptor and is the hospital's answer for a refractory beta-blocked patient.

checks.q: A 10 kg toddler has anaphylaxis and you carry only adult 0.3 mg and pediatric 0.15 mg auto-injectors, plus a 1 mg/mL vial and syringes under your protocol. What is the best option?
choices: Draw 0.01 mg/kg, which is 0.1 mg, or 0.1 mL of the 1 mg/mL concentration
Give the 0.3 mg adult device
Give half of the 0.15 mg device
Withhold epinephrine because the child is under 15 kg
checks.why: At 10 kg the weight-based dose is 0.1 mg. Auto-injectors cannot be partially delivered, the adult device is triple the dose with too long a needle, and withholding epinephrine in anaphylaxis is never correct.

checks.q: A 16-year-old ate a food she is allergic to, then vomited repeatedly and became lightheaded with a BP of 82/44. Her skin is completely clear. What is the correct action?
choices: Wait for hives before treating as anaphylaxis
Treat as anaphylaxis and give 0.3 mg epinephrine IM in the thigh
Give only oral fluids and monitor
Treat as simple food poisoning
checks.why: Roughly one in five anaphylactic reactions has no skin findings. A known exposure plus gastrointestinal symptoms plus hypotension meets the definition, and she weighs over 30 kg, so the adult dose applies.

lessons.title: Naloxone in the populations that complicate it
lessons.body:
Naloxone is close to risk-free in a naive patient who overdosed once. It is not risk-free in the people you actually meet, and the differences change how much you give and what you do next.

## The chronic pain patient

A patient on long-term morphine, methadone or a fentanyl patch is physically dependent. Slam the receptors clear and you produce instant, total withdrawal: vomiting, tearing pain, agitation, a hypertensive surge, and in rare cases flash pulmonary edema. You also take away the only thing controlling severe pain, and the hospital cannot easily put it back.

The fix is to treat what is actually dangerous. Open the airway and ventilate first. Then use the **smallest effective amount** — at the ALS level that means `0.04 to 0.4 mg` titrated intravenously; with the intranasal devices you carry, it means giving one dose, ventilating, and waiting the full `2 to 3 minutes` before deciding on another.

> **Key:** The goal is breathing, not conversation. Roughly `12` breaths a minute with good chest rise is a success. A patient who sits up furious is an overshoot.

## Fentanyl and its analogs

Fentanyl is `50 to 100` times more potent than morphine, and carfentanil far beyond that. Two practical consequences:

- **Repeat dosing is normal.** Two, three or four doses at `2 to 3 minute` intervals is common, and it does not mean the first ones failed.
- **Chest wall rigidity.** High-dose fentanyl can stiffen the chest and abdominal muscles so that bagging feels impossible. Do not conclude the airway is obstructed. Use two-person bag-valve-mask technique with a good seal and an airway adjunct, keep ventilating, and give naloxone, which reverses the rigidity.

Skin contact with street fentanyl does not cause overdose in a responder. Gloves and not touching your face are enough; panic on scene delays the patient's ventilation.

## The combative wake-up

Plan for it before you give the dose. Move sharps out of reach, position yourself at the head rather than leaning over the chest, have suction ready because vomiting is common, and brief your partner and any police on scene about what is coming and why. When the patient wakes, expect anger, name what happened in plain language, and do not argue. Most agitation is withdrawal, not hostility.

Refusal is the real hazard. Naloxone lasts `30 to 90 minutes` and most opioids last longer, so a patient who refuses transport may stop breathing within the hour. Involve medical direction, document the capacity assessment and the risks you described, leave the patient with someone who can call `911`, and where your system supports it, leave a naloxone kit.

## Populations with a different answer

- **Pregnancy.** Naloxone can precipitate withdrawal in the fetus and trigger preterm labor. Ventilate, titrate to breathing only, and transport — do not aim for full wakefulness.
- **The newborn of an opioid-dependent mother.** Naloxone is **not** used in newborn resuscitation; it can cause seizures in an exposed infant. Warm, dry, stimulate and ventilate at `40 to 60` breaths per minute instead.
- **Buprenorphine (Suboxone).** It grips the receptor tightly, so standard naloxone doses may barely move it. Ventilate and expect to repeat.
- **Polysubstance.** Naloxone does nothing for benzodiazepines, alcohol, gabapentin or stimulants. If two or three doses produce no change in breathing, stop assuming opioids and keep managing the airway while you look for another cause — head injury, low glucose, or a clonidine ingestion, which also causes pinpoint pupils.

> **On shift:** In New Jersey, naloxone is available at every level of EMS, to law enforcement and to the public, and the Good Samaritan provisions protect callers. Ask how much was given before you arrived and add it to your total.
keyPoints: Ventilate first; titrate naloxone to adequate breathing of about 12 per minute, never to full alertness.
Chronic pain and dependent patients need the smallest effective dose to avoid precipitated withdrawal and uncontrolled pain.
Fentanyl analogs often need repeated doses and can cause chest wall rigidity that makes bagging difficult until reversed.
Naloxone is not used in newborn resuscitation and is titrated to breathing only in pregnancy.
Naloxone lasts 30 to 90 minutes, less than most opioids, so refusal after reversal is a high-risk decision requiring medical direction and documentation.

checks.q: A 58-year-old on a fentanyl patch for cancer pain is breathing 6 times a minute with pinpoint pupils. What is the best approach?
choices: Give 4 mg intranasal naloxone immediately to wake him fully
Ventilate with a bag-valve mask first, then give the smallest effective naloxone dose and titrate to breathing
Withhold naloxone entirely because he is a pain patient
Remove the patch and wait for the drug to wear off
checks.why: Hypoxia is what kills, so ventilation comes first. Full reversal in a dependent patient causes severe withdrawal and uncontrolled pain, so the target is adequate respirations, not wakefulness. The patch should also be removed, but that alone is far too slow.

checks.q: You have given three doses of naloxone to an unresponsive patient with no change in respirations. What should you conclude?
choices: A fourth dose will certainly work
The naloxone is expired
Something other than opioids may be responsible, so keep ventilating and look for another cause
The patient is beyond help
checks.why: Naloxone does nothing for benzodiazepines, alcohol, stimulants, head injury or hypoglycemia. Continue ventilation and airway management and broaden the differential rather than repeating the same intervention.

checks.q: A newborn delivered to a mother who uses heroin is apneic and limp. What is the correct treatment?
choices: Naloxone 0.1 mg/kg intramuscularly
Naloxone intranasally, half the adult dose
Nothing until the heart rate falls below 60
Warm, dry, stimulate, position, and ventilate at 40 to 60 breaths per minute; do not give naloxone
checks.why: Naloxone is not part of newborn resuscitation and can cause seizures in an opioid-exposed infant. Newborn depression is corrected with warmth, stimulation and effective ventilation.

lessons.title: Aspirin and nitroglycerin: the edge cases
lessons.body:
The straightforward chest pain call is `324 mg` chewed and a nitroglycerin dose with a pressure check. These are the versions where the right answer is not the reflex.

## Aspirin edge cases

**Already anticoagulated.** A patient on apixaban or warfarin with suspected acute coronary syndrome still gets aspirin in most protocols. The two drugs work on different parts of clotting, and the benefit in a growing coronary clot outweighs the bleeding risk. Say the anticoagulant out loud at the hospital.

**Allergy versus intolerance.** "Aspirin upsets my stomach" is not an allergy. Hives, facial swelling, or wheezing after aspirin is. The one pattern to respect is **aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease**: asthma plus nasal polyps plus a history of wheezing after aspirin or ibuprofen. That patient does not get aspirin.

**Nothing but enteric-coated available.** The coating exists to slow absorption, the opposite of what you want. Chewing enteric-coated tablets thoroughly is better than nothing when it is all there is, but plain chewable `81 mg` tablets are the standard and what your kit should hold. Varies by protocol.

**Cannot chew.** A vomiting patient, an altered patient, or one who cannot protect the airway does not get oral aspirin. Document that you withheld it and why.

**A suspected tear of the aorta.** Tearing pain radiating to the back, a blood pressure difference between arms, or a pulse deficit changes the picture. Blood thinning is unhelpful there, so follow protocol and flag the suspicion early rather than quietly giving the aspirin.

**Children and teenagers with a fever or viral illness** never get aspirin, because of Reye syndrome.

## Nitroglycerin edge cases

**The bottle that no longer works.** Sublingual tablets degrade with heat, light and air. A bottle opened more than `3 to 6 months` ago, kept in a car or a pocket, may be inert. The old teaching that a burning or fizzing sensation under the tongue proves potency is unreliable. If three doses of the patient's own tablets change nothing, consider the bottle rather than concluding the pain is not cardiac.

**Doses already taken.** Count what the patient took before you arrived toward the maximum of `3`. A patient who took two at home gets one more from you, not three.

**Right ventricular infarction.** An inferior wall myocardial infarction often involves the right ventricle, which depends on filling volume to work at all. Nitroglycerin drops that volume and can cause a sudden, profound drop in pressure. If the pressure crashes after a dose, lie the patient flat, elevate the legs, give oxygen if saturations are low, and request ALS for fluid.

**Nitroglycerin patches.** A patch is still delivering drug. If the patient is hypotensive, remove it with a gloved hand and wipe the skin. Remove a patch before defibrillation pads go anywhere near it, because the backing can arc and burn.

**Cocaine-associated chest pain** is one place nitroglycerin is genuinely helpful, because cocaine constricts coronary arteries.

**Head injury or suspected bleeding in the brain** is a contraindication: dilating vessels raises pressure inside the skull.

> **Trap:** The interaction question does not care why the drug was prescribed. Sildenafil as Revatio and tadalafil as Adcirca are prescribed for pulmonary hypertension to men and women of any age. Ask about "any medication for circulation, the lungs, or erections in the last two days," not about erectile dysfunction alone.

> **Key:** The two checks before every dose never change: a systolic above `100 mmHg` per protocol measured right now, and no PDE-5 inhibitor within `24 hours`, or `48 hours` for tadalafil.

Reassess after each dose: pain score, blood pressure, heart rate and mental status, all with times. Pain that does not move after three doses is an emergency transport with early notification.
keyPoints: Anticoagulated patients still receive aspirin for suspected ACS in most protocols; stomach upset is intolerance, not allergy.
Asthma with nasal polyps and prior wheezing after aspirin or NSAIDs is a genuine contraindication.
Count nitroglycerin doses taken before your arrival toward the maximum of 3, and recheck the pressure before each dose.
Inferior or right ventricular infarction depends on preload, so nitroglycerin can cause a profound pressure drop; lay flat, elevate the legs, request ALS.
Sublingual tablets lose potency after 3 to 6 months of an opened bottle, and a burning sensation does not prove potency.

checks.q: A 66-year-old with crushing chest pain takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. What should you do about aspirin?
choices: Withhold aspirin because he is already anticoagulated
Give 324 mg chewed per protocol and report the apixaban at the hospital
Give 81 mg only
Give aspirin only if his blood pressure is above 100 systolic
checks.why: Aspirin blocks platelets while apixaban blocks a clotting factor, and most protocols still give the full dose for suspected ACS. The pressure rule belongs to nitroglycerin, not aspirin.

checks.q: A patient with chest pain took two of his own nitroglycerin tablets before you arrived. His current BP is 118/72 and the pain persists. How many more may you assist with?
choices: Three more, because your count starts now
None, because he self-administered
One more, to reach the maximum of three total
As many as needed until the pain resolves
checks.why: Doses taken before your arrival count toward the maximum of three. Recheck the blood pressure before that dose and reassess afterward.

checks.q: After one nitroglycerin dose in a patient with an inferior wall infarction, BP drops from 116/70 to 78/44 and he feels faint. What do you do?
choices: Lay him flat, elevate the legs, withhold further nitroglycerin, give oxygen if saturations are low, and request ALS
Give a second dose to relieve the pain
Sit him upright to ease his breathing
Give aspirin to raise the blood pressure
checks.why: A right ventricle starved of filling volume drops output sharply when preload falls. Restore preload with position and fluids from ALS, and give no more nitroglycerin.

lessons.title: When the patient cannot take oral glucose
lessons.body:
Oral glucose has one gate: can this person swallow and protect their own airway? When the answer is no, smearing gel into the cheek is not a workaround. It is aspiration with extra steps, and the old teaching that it absorbs through the buccal lining in a meaningful amount is wrong — absorption that way is slow and trivial.

So the question becomes what else there is.

## Glucagon

Glucagon is a hormone that tells the liver to release its stored sugar (glycogen). It works without an IV and without the patient swallowing, which is why it exists in a home kit and in an expanding number of EMS protocols.

- **Dose:** `1 mg` intramuscular for patients about `25 kg` and above; `0.5 mg` for smaller children. Intranasal glucagon is `3 mg` in one nostril and works even with a blocked nose.
- **Preparation:** the traditional kit is a powder vial and a syringe of diluent. Inject the diluent into the powder, swirl gently until clear, and draw the dose back up. Prefilled auto-injector versions need no mixing.
- **Onset:** `8 to 15 minutes`, sometimes `20`. That is slow when a brain has no fuel, so it is a bridge to ALS or the hospital, not a finish line.
- **Expect vomiting.** Nausea and vomiting are the main side effects. Position the patient on their side and keep suction in your hand.
- **When it fails:** glucagon needs a liver with glycogen in it. In chronic alcohol use, starvation, liver disease or a prolonged hypoglycemic episode, the shelves are empty and glucagon does little. Those patients need intravenous dextrose.

> **Key:** Glucagon unlocks a storeroom. Dextrose delivers the sugar itself. If the storeroom is empty, only dextrose works.

## Dextrose

At the ALS level, `25 g` of dextrose is given intravenously, either as `50 mL` of `D50` or, increasingly preferred, `250 mL` of `D10`, which is gentler on the vein and less likely to overshoot. Children are dosed by weight, commonly `5 mL/kg` of `D10`. Your role is recognizing the need, getting the ALS request out early, and having a glucose number and a time to hand over.

## Devices on the patient

**Insulin pumps** keep delivering insulin during hypoglycemia unless someone stops them. Ask the patient or the family to suspend or disconnect it — they know their device. Do not start pressing buttons on hardware you have never used, and never remove an infusion set on your own unless your protocol says so. Note the time it was stopped.

**Continuous glucose sensors** read the fluid between cells, not blood, so they lag capillary glucose by `5 to 15 minutes` and can be badly wrong during a fast fall. Treat the patient and confirm with a fingerstick.

## The other traps

- **Never** put glucose, juice, candy or food into the mouth of a seizing, unresponsive or gagging patient.
- **Hypoglycemia unawareness** develops in long-standing diabetics and in patients on beta blockers, who lose the tremor and pounding heart that would normally warn them. They go from fine to unconscious with almost no warning.
- **Once the patient is awake**, a complex carbohydrate plus protein — a sandwich, not a soda — prevents the second drop.
- **The refusal after recovery.** Recheck the glucose before you release anyone, and transport the patient on a sulfonylurea such as glipizide or glyburide, on long-acting insulin, or with no food and nobody at home. Those lows come back after you leave.

> **On shift:** Document the glucose value and the time for every reading, the route and time of whatever you gave, the pump status, and the number at the moment of transfer or release. That timeline is the story of the call.
keyPoints: Oral glucose requires an intact swallow and airway; buccal absorption in an unresponsive patient is a myth and an aspiration risk.
Glucagon is 1 mg IM for about 25 kg and above, 0.5 mg for smaller children, 3 mg intranasally, with onset in 8 to 15 minutes and vomiting expected.
Glucagon fails when liver glycogen is depleted, as in alcohol use, starvation or liver disease; those patients need IV dextrose.
ALS dextrose is 25 g as 50 mL of D50 or 250 mL of D10, with pediatric dosing about 5 mL/kg of D10.
Ask the patient or family to suspend an insulin pump, and confirm a continuous sensor reading with a fingerstick because it lags by 5 to 15 minutes.

checks.q: A diabetic is unresponsive with a glucose of 29 mg/dL and no gag reflex. Your service carries glucagon. What is the correct sequence?
choices: Place oral glucose gel between the cheek and gum and monitor
Manage the airway and ventilation, give glucagon 1 mg IM, position on the side for vomiting, and request ALS
Give glucagon and then oral glucose together
Wait for ALS without intervening
checks.why: Nothing goes in the mouth of a patient who cannot protect the airway. Glucagon works without swallowing but takes 8 to 15 minutes and commonly causes vomiting, so airway control and positioning come with it.

checks.q: A patient with long-standing alcohol use is hypoglycemic and unresponsive. Why might glucagon fail?
choices: Alcohol blocks glucagon receptors directly
Glucagon requires an intravenous line to work
Glucagon releases stored liver glycogen, and chronic alcohol use leaves those stores depleted
Glucagon only works in type 1 diabetes
checks.why: Glucagon mobilizes glycogen. With little or no glycogen in the liver there is nothing to mobilize, so intravenous dextrose is required.

checks.q: A hypoglycemic patient wearing an insulin pump is now awake after treatment. What should you do about the pump?
choices: Leave it running so his sugar does not rise too high
Remove the infusion set yourself immediately
Ignore it, since a pump cannot cause hypoglycemia
Ask the patient or family to suspend or disconnect it, and record the time it was stopped
checks.why: A pump continues delivering insulin through a low unless someone stops it. The user knows the device far better than you do, and the time it was suspended matters to the hospital.

lessons.title: Expanded scope: what you carry when the state says yes
lessons.body:
"Can an EMT give that?" has four answers stacked on top of each other, and all four have to be yes.

1. **The national scope model** describes what an EMT can be trained to do. It is a floor, not a license.
2. **The state** writes the actual list into statute or regulation. New Jersey's Office of Emergency Medical Services does this for New Jersey.
3. **Your agency's medical director** adopts a protocol that puts the drug in your bag and defines the indication, the dose and whether you need to call.
4. **You** hold a current credential for it, including any additional training and quality-assurance requirements the program demands.

> **Key:** On the NREMT, answer from the national standard of care. On the street, answer from your protocol. In your documentation, write the authority: "per standing order 4-2" or "per NJ OEMS protocol."

## The commonly added items

**Glucagon** `1 mg` IM, or `3 mg` intranasally, for hypoglycemia in a patient who cannot take anything by mouth. This is the single most common expansion, because it turns a wait-for-ALS call into a treatment.

**Epinephrine drawn from a vial** rather than an auto-injector. New Jersey runs an EMT epinephrine program on exactly this model: `1 mg/mL` concentration, `0.3 mg` (which is `0.3 mL`) for adults, `0.15 mg` for `15 to 30 kg`. Cheaper than devices, but it moves the dose calculation onto you, which is why these programs come with extra training and chart review.

**Nebulized albuterol** administered by the EMT, as opposed to assisting with the patient's own inhaler. Where authorized it is the standard `2.5 mg` in `3 mL` at `6 to 8 L/min`, sometimes with ipratropium added.

**Acetaminophen or ibuprofen** for pain or fever, and **ondansetron** `4 mg` dissolving tablet for nausea, exist in a growing number of systems. **Nitrous oxide**, self-administered `50/50` with oxygen, exists in a few.

## CPAP as a therapy, not a gadget

Continuous positive airway pressure is the expanded intervention that saves the most lives, and it behaves like a drug: it has a dose, an onset, a failure point and a side effect profile.

**Mechanism.** Constant pressure holds small airways and air sacs open through the whole cycle, pushes fluid out of the air sacs back into circulation, and reduces the work of breathing. In heart failure it also reduces the volume returning to the heart, which unloads a failing pump.

**Dose.** Start at `5 cm H2O` and titrate to `10`, per protocol, with oxygen blended to hold saturations at target.

**Coaching is the skill.** Hold the mask on gently with your hand for the first minute and talk the patient through it before any straps go on. A panicking patient will fight a strapped mask and lose.

**Watch for.** Falling blood pressure as the pressure reduces venous return, gastric distension and vomiting, claustrophobia, and a dry mouth.

**Failure criteria.** If mental status declines, the patient cannot cooperate, vomiting begins, the pressure drops, or saturations are not improving after `5 to 10 minutes`, stop and ventilate with a bag-valve mask. Keep the device on through hallway transfers and the switch to the hospital bed — the crash usually happens when somebody takes it off "for a second."

> **On shift:** Whatever the added skill, three things travel with it: written authorization you can name, a documented indication, and a reassessment with a time. Expanded scope is not permission to improvise.
keyPoints: Four layers authorize any EMT medication: national scope, state law, the medical director's protocol, and your own credential.
Common expansions are glucagon, epinephrine by syringe from a 1 mg/mL vial, EMT-administered nebulized albuterol, and in some systems ondansetron or analgesics.
CPAP starts at 5 cm H2O and titrates to about 10, with coaching as the actual skill.
Stop CPAP and bag the patient for declining mental status, vomiting, hypotension, or no improvement in 5 to 10 minutes.
Document the authority for every expanded-scope intervention by protocol number or physician name.

checks.q: A patient in severe pulmonary edema has been on CPAP at 10 cm H2O for eight minutes. He is becoming harder to rouse and his systolic has fallen from 168 to 96. What should you do?
choices: Increase the pressure to 15 cm H2O
Remove CPAP and begin bag-valve-mask ventilation, and treat the hypotension
Strap the mask tighter to improve the seal
Continue unchanged, since a falling pressure is expected
checks.why: Declining mental status and hypotension are both CPAP failure criteria. Positive pressure reduces venous return, and a patient who cannot protect the airway cannot stay on the device.

checks.q: Your protocol authorizes epinephrine by syringe. You pick up a vial labeled 1 mg/mL for an adult with anaphylaxis. What do you draw and give?
choices: 3 mL intramuscularly in the thigh
0.3 mL intramuscularly in the thigh
0.3 mL intravenously
1 mL intramuscularly in the deltoid
checks.why: 0.3 mg divided by 1 mg/mL is 0.3 mL, given intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh. Three milliliters would be 3 mg, and intravenous epinephrine at this concentration is not an EMT intervention.

lessons.title: Medication errors, reporting, and just culture
lessons.body:
You will make an error. The measure of a clinician is not whether it happens but what happens in the next five minutes.

## Where errors actually come from

Errors cluster in predictable places, and none of them are about caring less.

- **Look-alike, sound-alike drugs.** Hydralazine and hydroxyzine. Epinephrine `1 mg/mL` and `0.1 mg/mL` in near-identical boxes. Two strengths of the same auto-injector in the same pouch.
- **The decimal point.** `0.15` read as `1.5` is a tenfold overdose. Always write a leading zero and never a trailing one: `0.3 mg`, not `.3 mg` and not `0.30 mg`.
- **Weight-based pediatric dosing** done from memory under pressure.
- **Interruption.** Most drug errors happen during a conversation, a radio call or a scene move.
- **Assumption.** "It was in the pediatric pouch, so it must be the pediatric dose."

## What you do the moment you realize

1. **Patient first.** Reassess airway, breathing, circulation and mental status, take a full set of vitals, and treat the effect. A doubled epinephrine dose means monitoring for tachycardia, chest pain and severe hypertension; a missed dose means giving it now if still indicated.
2. **Say it out loud to your partner** and to ALS if they are on scene. Concealment is what turns an error into harm.
3. **Tell the receiving nurse and physician explicitly**, in the handoff, with the drug, the dose, the route and the time. Do not bury it in the chart and hope it gets read.
4. **Document facts, not blame.** What was given, how much, by what route, at what time, what you observed afterward, what you did, and who you notified. No speculation, no adjectives, no naming fault.
5. **Never alter a record.** On paper, a single line through the entry with your initials, the date and the reason. Electronically, an addendum with its own timestamp. Rewriting a chart after the fact is a far more serious problem than the error it was hiding.
6. **File the report** your agency requires — an incident or quality-assurance form — even when nothing bad happened. Near-misses are the cheapest data in medicine.

> **Key:** The patient needs assessment and honesty, in that order and quickly. Everything else is paperwork that can be done carefully afterward.

## Just culture

A just culture sorts behavior into three categories and responds differently to each, which is the whole point.

- **Human error** is a slip: the right intention, the wrong hand. The response is to console the person and fix the system that allowed it.
- **At-risk behavior** is drifting into an unsafe shortcut that has become normal, such as skipping the third label check because it has never mattered before. The response is coaching, and removing the incentive to cut that corner.
- **Reckless behavior** is a conscious disregard of a substantial risk — giving a medication while impaired, or falsifying a chart. That is the only category that belongs in discipline.

Systems, not lectures, prevent repeats: standardized drug kits with one concentration per drug, color-coded pediatric tapes, read-backs of every verbal order, a two-person check on high-alert medications, saying the dose out loud before it goes in, and removing look-alike packaging from the bag entirely.

> **On shift:** Expect to feel terrible afterward. That reaction is well described in clinicians who harm a patient by accident, and it is why agencies have peer support and employee assistance programs. Use them, and do not work the rest of a shift pretending it did not happen.
keyPoints: Errors cluster around look-alike drugs, decimal points, weight-based pediatric doses, interruptions and assumptions.
After an error: reassess and treat the patient, tell your partner, tell the receiving provider explicitly, document facts, and file the report.
Never alter a record; correct on paper with a single line, initials and date, or electronically with a timestamped addendum.
Just culture separates human error (console), at-risk behavior (coach) and reckless behavior (discipline).
Prevention is structural: one concentration per drug, read-backs, two-person checks on high-alert drugs, and saying the dose out loud.

checks.q: You realize you gave a 22 kg child the 0.3 mg adult epinephrine auto-injector instead of the 0.15 mg pediatric device. What is your first action?
choices: Reassess the patient, take a full set of vitals, and monitor for tachycardia, hypertension and chest discomfort
Finish the call and file a report at the station
Document it in the chart and say nothing at handoff
Ask your partner not to mention it
checks.why: The patient comes first. After reassessing and treating the effect, you tell your partner, tell the receiving nurse and physician explicitly, document objectively, and file the quality-assurance report.

checks.q: Under just culture, how is a single unintentional slip by a well-trained EMT handled?
choices: Immediate suspension, because patient safety is absolute
As human error: support the provider and fix the system conditions that allowed it
It is ignored entirely so people are not discouraged from reporting
The same way as falsifying a chart
checks.why: Just culture separates human error from at-risk behavior and recklessness. Punishing slips drives reporting underground, which removes the data needed to prevent the next one. Falsifying a record is reckless and is handled very differently.

checks.q: You wrote the wrong administration time in a paper patient care report. How do you correct it?
choices: Erase it and write the correct time
Use correction fluid so the chart stays legible
Draw a single line through the entry, write the correction, and add your initials and the date
Leave it, since the time is minor
checks.why: A record must show what was originally written and what changed. A single line with initials and date preserves the original; erasing or covering an entry looks like concealment and is a far larger problem than the error.

cards.front: Which two emergencies does a beta blocker hide?
cards.back: The tachycardia of shock, and the tremor and palpitations of hypoglycemia. Sweating still occurs. Judge perfusion by skin, mental status and capillary refill, and check a glucose on anyone who seems off.

cards.front: Why does an anticoagulated patient with a minor head strike still need transport?
cards.back: Bleeding in the brain can start slowly and declare itself 6 to 72 hours later. A normal exam on scene does not exclude it, and the drug prevents the bleed from stopping on its own.

cards.front: Why does long-acting insulin cause 3 a.m. hypoglycemia?
cards.back: Glargine and similar insulins are dosed for a normal eating day. A skipped meal, a vomiting illness, or new exercise leaves the insulin working with no incoming glucose, hours after the last dose.

cards.front: What happens when an MAO inhibitor meets a sympathomimetic?
cards.back: Hypertensive crisis. Phenelzine, tranylcypromine or selegiline plus pseudoephedrine, amphetamines, cocaine or aged foods produces a sudden severe headache, a systolic over 200, chest pain and stroke risk.

cards.front: How do you recognize serotonin syndrome, and how does it differ from neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
cards.back: Serotonin syndrome: agitation, clonus and hyperreflexia, fever and diarrhea, developing over hours after adding a serotonergic drug. NMS follows antipsychotics over days with lead-pipe rigidity and slowed reflexes.

cards.front: Why does a diuretic make digoxin dangerous?
cards.back: Furosemide and hydrochlorothiazide lower potassium, and low potassium makes the heart more sensitive to digoxin. A stable dose turns toxic: nausea, confusion, yellow-green halos, slow or irregular rhythms.

cards.front: How does ACE inhibitor angioedema differ from anaphylaxis?
cards.back: Lips and tongue swell with no hives and no itching, it is not histamine-driven, and it responds poorly to epinephrine and antihistamines. It can start years into therapy. Give epinephrine anyway for a threatened airway.

cards.front: What does metoprolol plus furosemide plus lisinopril plus spironolactone tell you?
cards.back: Heart failure with reduced pumping. Expect fluid overload, orthopnea and weight gain, and remember the beta blocker will keep the heart rate from rising.

cards.front: What does apixaban plus diltiazem plus digoxin suggest?
cards.back: Atrial fibrillation. Expect an irregular pulse, an elevated bleeding risk with any trauma, and digoxin toxicity if potassium has fallen.

cards.front: Why does months of daily prednisone change your thinking?
cards.back: The adrenal glands stop producing their own stress hormone. Infection, injury or vomiting can cause adrenal crisis: weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain and hypotension that does not respond to position. They need hospital steroids.

cards.front: Why is a fever an emergency in a patient on methotrexate, adalimumab or clozapine?
cards.back: All three suppress the immune system or the white cell count. Infection can progress rapidly with unimpressive early findings, and clozapine can wipe out the cells that fight it entirely.

cards.front: What do Revatio and Adcirca tell you, and why does it matter?
cards.back: They are sildenafil and tadalafil prescribed for pulmonary hypertension, in patients of any age or sex. They contraindicate nitroglycerin for 24 and 48 hours respectively, and nobody volunteers them when you ask about erectile dysfunction drugs.

cards.front: What does a bottle of 30 tablets filled 40 days ago with 25 left tell you?
cards.back: The patient is barely taking the medication. Nonadherence explains a large share of seizure, hypertensive, psychiatric and heart failure calls. Report the count, not just the drug.

cards.front: Why does a medication started in the last two weeks matter?
cards.back: A new drug or a dose change is the leading suspect for today's problem, whether through a side effect, an interaction, or a drop in standing blood pressure. Ask specifically what is new.

cards.front: What does buprenorphine-naloxone or methadone on a medication list imply for care?
cards.back: Opioid use disorder in treatment. Expect high opioid tolerance, treat the patient respectfully, and know that buprenorphine grips the receptor tightly so naloxone works poorly against it.

cards.front: Convert 33 lb and 154 lb to kilograms.
cards.back: 33 divided by 2.2 is 15 kg, the bottom of the pediatric auto-injector band. 154 divided by 2.2 is 70 kg. Field estimate: halve the pounds and subtract 10 percent.

cards.front: From a 1 mg/mL epinephrine vial, what volumes give 0.3 mg and 0.15 mg?
cards.back: 0.3 mL and 0.15 mL. Volume equals dose divided by concentration. From a 0.1 mg/mL vial the same 0.3 mg would take 3 mL, which is the wrong product for an IM anaphylaxis dose.

cards.front: What is the weight-based pediatric epinephrine dose and how do you draw it?
cards.back: 0.01 mg/kg of the 1 mg/mL concentration, usually capped at 0.3 mg. A 12 kg child needs 0.12 mg, which is 0.12 mL.

cards.front: How many 81 mg chewable tablets make the prehospital aspirin dose, and how much nitroglycerin is three doses?
cards.back: Four tablets chewed for 324 mg of aspirin. Three nitroglycerin doses of 0.4 mg total 1.2 mg, with a blood pressure check before each one.

cards.front: How many grams of dextrose are in 50 mL of D50 and in 250 mL of D10?
cards.back: 25 g in both. A percent solution is grams per 100 mL, so D50 is 0.5 g/mL and D10 is 0.1 g/mL. D10 is gentler on the vein for the same dose.

cards.front: How much sodium chloride is in a 1,000 mL bag of 0.9% saline?
cards.back: 9 grams. A percent solution means grams per 100 mL, so 0.9 g per 100 mL times ten is 9 g per liter.

cards.front: What is the formula for oxygen cylinder duration, and the cylinder constants?
cards.back: Minutes equal pressure minus a 200 psi residual, times the constant, divided by flow. D is 0.16, E is 0.28, M is 1.56. An E cylinder at 1,800 psi running 15 L/min lasts about 30 minutes.

cards.front: Why is the decimal point the most dangerous character in a dose?
cards.back: 0.15 read as 1.5 is a tenfold overdose. Always write a leading zero and never a trailing zero: 0.3 mg, not .3 mg and not 0.30 mg. Say the number out loud before giving it.

cards.front: How does a beta blocker change an anaphylaxis call?
cards.back: Beta receptors are partially blocked, so airway opening and cardiac output response are blunted and one dose is more likely to be insufficient. Repeat epinephrine, call ALS, and tell the hospital so glucagon can be considered.

cards.front: What is the hospital's answer for anaphylaxis that does not respond in a beta-blocked patient?
cards.back: Glucagon 1 to 5 mg intravenously. It raises cardiac output through a receptor the beta blocker does not occupy. This is an ALS or hospital intervention, not a BLS one.

cards.front: Does a cardiac history or advanced age change the epinephrine dose in anaphylaxis?
cards.back: No. Give the standard 0.3 mg IM in the thigh. Untreated anaphylaxis kills in minutes, while harm from IM epinephrine is rare. Monitor closely and expect tachycardia.

cards.front: List the pediatric epinephrine weight bands.
cards.back: 7.5 to 15 kg: a 0.1 mg device where available, or 0.01 mg/kg drawn up. 15 to 30 kg: 0.15 mg. 30 kg and above: 0.3 mg. Under 7.5 kg, draw it up rather than using a device.

cards.front: What technique errors are specific to auto-injectors in children?
cards.back: Failing to hold the leg still, which causes thigh lacerations; injecting through a pocket with objects in it; and holding the device by the needle end. Use the outer middle third of the thigh at 90 degrees.

cards.front: What do you do about an accidental auto-injector injection into your thumb?
cards.back: The digit turns white, cold and numb from vasoconstriction. Keep the hand warm, note the time, and get it evaluated at an emergency department.

cards.front: Can anaphylaxis occur without hives?
cards.back: Yes. Roughly one in five reactions has no skin findings. A known exposure plus airway symptoms, vomiting, or hypotension is anaphylaxis, and waiting for a rash costs lives.

cards.front: Why give the smallest effective naloxone dose to a chronic pain patient?
cards.back: Full reversal causes instant withdrawal: vomiting, agitation, a hypertensive surge, rarely flash pulmonary edema, and the loss of pain control that the hospital cannot easily restore. Ventilate first and titrate to breathing.

cards.front: Why do fentanyl overdoses often need several naloxone doses?
cards.back: Fentanyl is 50 to 100 times more potent than morphine and analogs are stronger still. Two to four doses at 2 to 3 minute intervals is common and does not mean the earlier doses failed.

cards.front: What is fentanyl chest wall rigidity and how do you manage it?
cards.back: High-dose fentanyl stiffens chest and abdominal muscles so bagging feels obstructed. Use two-person bag-valve-mask technique with an airway adjunct, keep ventilating, and give naloxone, which reverses it.

cards.front: How do you prepare for a combative naloxone wake-up?
cards.back: Move sharps out of reach, position at the head rather than over the chest, have suction ready, and brief your partner and police before the dose. Expect withdrawal-driven anger, and do not argue.

cards.front: Why is naloxone used differently in pregnancy?
cards.back: It can precipitate fetal withdrawal and trigger preterm labor. Ventilate, titrate only to adequate maternal breathing, and transport rather than aiming for full wakefulness.

cards.front: What is the role of naloxone in newborn resuscitation?
cards.back: None. It can cause seizures in an opioid-exposed newborn. Warm, dry, stimulate, position and ventilate at 40 to 60 breaths per minute instead.

cards.front: Three naloxone doses produce no change in breathing. What now?
cards.back: Stop assuming opioids. Naloxone does nothing for benzodiazepines, alcohol, gabapentin or stimulants. Keep ventilating and consider head injury, hypoglycemia or a clonidine ingestion, which also causes pinpoint pupils.

cards.front: Does a patient on apixaban or warfarin still get aspirin for chest pain?
cards.back: Yes in most protocols. Aspirin blocks platelets while anticoagulants block clotting factors, and the benefit in a growing coronary clot outweighs the bleeding risk. Report the anticoagulant at the hospital.

cards.front: How do you distinguish aspirin allergy from aspirin intolerance?
cards.back: Stomach upset or heartburn is intolerance and not a contraindication. Hives, facial swelling or wheezing is allergy. Respect asthma with nasal polyps and prior wheezing after aspirin or NSAIDs as a true contraindication.

cards.front: Why are enteric-coated aspirin tablets a poor choice in a heart attack?
cards.back: The coating exists to delay absorption, which is the opposite of the goal. Plain chewable 81 mg tablets, chewed, are the standard; chewing enteric tablets is a fallback when nothing else is available.

cards.front: How do doses the patient took before you arrived affect the nitroglycerin maximum?
cards.back: They count. Three total doses is the usual maximum, so a patient who took two at home may receive one more, with a blood pressure check before it.

cards.front: Why can nitroglycerin crash the pressure in an inferior wall MI?
cards.back: Inferior infarcts often involve the right ventricle, which depends on filling volume. Nitroglycerin drops that volume. If the pressure falls, lay the patient flat, elevate the legs, and request ALS for fluid.

cards.front: What should you do with a nitroglycerin patch you find on a patient?
cards.back: It is still delivering drug. Remove it with a gloved hand and wipe the skin if the patient is hypotensive, and always remove it before defibrillation pads go near it, because the backing can arc and burn.

cards.front: How long do sublingual nitroglycerin tablets stay potent, and does burning prove potency?
cards.back: An opened bottle degrades over about 3 to 6 months, faster with heat and light. A burning or tingling sensation under the tongue is not a reliable potency test, so consider an inert bottle if three doses do nothing.

cards.front: Which chest pain causes make nitroglycerin unhelpful or unsafe?
cards.back: Head injury or suspected bleeding in the brain, hypotension, a recent PDE-5 inhibitor, and a suspected tear of the aorta. Cocaine-associated chest pain is one case where nitroglycerin genuinely helps.

cards.front: Why is putting glucose gel in the cheek of an unresponsive patient wrong?
cards.back: Buccal absorption is slow and trivial, and a patient who cannot protect the airway will aspirate it. The gate for oral glucose is the ability to swallow, not the glucose number.

cards.front: What are the glucagon doses and routes?
cards.back: 1 mg intramuscularly at about 25 kg and above, 0.5 mg for smaller children, or 3 mg intranasally in one nostril. Onset is 8 to 15 minutes, and vomiting is the main side effect.

cards.front: How do you prepare a traditional glucagon kit?
cards.back: Inject the syringe of diluent into the powder vial, swirl gently until the solution is clear, then draw the dose back up. Prefilled auto-injector and nasal versions need no mixing.

cards.front: In which patients does glucagon fail, and why?
cards.back: Chronic alcohol use, starvation, liver disease, or a prolonged low. Glucagon releases stored liver glycogen, and those patients have none left. They need intravenous dextrose.

cards.front: What are the ALS dextrose options for an adult and a child?
cards.back: 25 g given as 50 mL of D50 or 250 mL of D10, with D10 increasingly preferred for being gentler on the vein. Children get about 5 mL/kg of D10.

cards.front: What do you do about an insulin pump during hypoglycemia?
cards.back: It keeps delivering insulin unless someone stops it. Ask the patient or family to suspend or disconnect it, note the time, and do not operate an unfamiliar device or pull an infusion set on your own.

cards.front: Why confirm a continuous glucose sensor reading with a fingerstick?
cards.back: Sensors read the fluid between cells and lag capillary blood by 5 to 15 minutes, so they can read falsely normal during a fast fall. Treat the patient and verify with a fingerstick.

cards.front: What four layers have to agree before an EMT can give a medication?
cards.back: The national scope of practice model, state law or regulation, the agency medical director's protocol, and your own current credential for it. Document the authority by protocol number or physician name.

cards.front: Name four medications commonly added to EMT scope where states allow it.
cards.back: Glucagon, epinephrine drawn from a 1 mg/mL vial, EMT-administered nebulized albuterol, and in some systems ondansetron 4 mg dissolving tablets or acetaminophen and ibuprofen.

cards.front: How does CPAP actually work?
cards.back: Constant pressure holds small airways and air sacs open, pushes fluid out of the air sacs back into circulation, and reduces work of breathing. In heart failure it also lowers the volume returning to the heart, unloading a failing pump.

cards.front: What are the starting settings and the coaching technique for CPAP?
cards.back: Start at 5 cm H2O and titrate to about 10 per protocol. Hold the mask on by hand for the first minute and explain it before any straps. A panicking patient will fight a strapped mask.

cards.front: What are the CPAP failure criteria?
cards.back: Declining mental status, inability to cooperate, vomiting, falling blood pressure, or no improvement in saturations after 5 to 10 minutes. Remove it and ventilate with a bag-valve mask.

cards.front: When is the most dangerous moment for a patient on CPAP?
cards.back: When someone takes it off for a transfer. Keep it on through hallway moves and the switch to the hospital bed until the receiving team is ready to take over.

cards.front: Where do medication errors actually come from?
cards.back: Look-alike and sound-alike drugs, decimal point misreads, weight-based pediatric doses done from memory, interruptions during administration, and assumptions about what is in a pouch.

cards.front: What are the first steps after you realize you made a medication error?
cards.back: Reassess and treat the patient, tell your partner and any ALS on scene, tell the receiving nurse and physician explicitly at handoff, document objectively, and file the incident or quality-assurance report.

cards.front: How do you correct an entry in a patient care report?
cards.back: On paper, draw a single line through it, write the correction, and add your initials and the date. Electronically, add a timestamped addendum. Never erase, cover, or rewrite a record.

cards.front: What are the three categories of just culture?
cards.back: Human error, which is consoled and met with a system fix; at-risk behavior, which is coached; and reckless behavior, a conscious disregard of serious risk, which is the only category that belongs in discipline.

cards.front: Which system fixes actually prevent medication errors?
cards.back: One concentration per drug in the kit, color-coded pediatric tapes, read-backs of verbal orders, two-person checks on high-alert drugs, saying the dose out loud, and removing look-alike packaging from the bag.

cards.front: Why report a near-miss that harmed nobody?
cards.back: Near-misses are the cheapest safety data available: they reveal the system flaw before it injures someone. Reporting them is also what keeps a just culture functioning.

quiz.q: A 74-year-old on metoprolol is found sweaty and confused. His heart rate is 68 and his skin is cool. Which explanation best fits, and what should you check first?
choices: He is anxious; check a blood pressure
The normal heart rate excludes hypoglycemia
The beta blocker removes the tremor and palpitations of hypoglycemia while sweating persists; check a glucose
He is having a stroke; no glucose check is needed
quiz.why: Beta-2 blockade removes the classic adrenergic warning signs of a low glucose, but sweating is driven by a different pathway and remains. A normal heart rate on a beta blocker is uninformative, and glucose is checked on every altered patient.

quiz.q: A patient on warfarin started ciprofloxacin four days ago and now has extensive bruising and a nosebleed that will not stop. What is the mechanism?
choices: The antibiotic increases the warfarin effect, raising bleeding risk
The antibiotic directly damages platelets
Warfarin becomes inactive with antibiotics, causing clotting
This is an allergic reaction to ciprofloxacin
quiz.why: Several antibiotics, including ciprofloxacin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and metronidazole, raise warfarin levels and prolong clotting within days. The patient needs evaluation and a clotting time check, not reassurance.

quiz.q: A patient taking phenelzine for depression took an over-the-counter cold medicine containing pseudoephedrine. He now has a severe headache, BP 224/128, and chest pain. What has happened?
choices: An allergic reaction to pseudoephedrine
A hypertensive crisis from an MAO inhibitor combined with a sympathomimetic
Serotonin syndrome
A panic attack with a false blood pressure reading
quiz.why: MAO inhibitors block the breakdown of norepinephrine, so an added sympathomimetic produces an uncontrolled pressor surge. Serotonin syndrome is a different picture, with clonus, fever and diarrhea rather than isolated severe hypertension.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old on lisinopril for six years wakes with a swollen tongue and lips. There are no hives, no itching, and no new exposures. What is the best interpretation and action?
choices: It cannot be the lisinopril after six years of use
It is an allergic reaction that will resolve with antihistamines alone
Give epinephrine and expect complete resolution within five minutes
It is ACE inhibitor angioedema, which responds poorly to epinephrine; give epinephrine anyway for a threatened airway and transport emergently
quiz.why: Angioedema from an ACE inhibitor is not histamine-driven, so the usual allergy drugs underperform, and it can appear years into therapy. You still give epinephrine because you cannot exclude anaphylaxis in the field, but the airway and the hospital are the real treatment.

quiz.q: A patient takes prednisone 10 mg daily for two years. He now has a vomiting illness with a BP of 84/50 that does not improve with position. What should you suspect?
choices: Simple dehydration from vomiting
Adrenal crisis from suppressed adrenal glands unable to mount a stress response
An allergic reaction to prednisone
Prednisone overdose
quiz.why: Chronic steroids shut down the body's own cortisol production. Illness or injury then produces weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain and refractory hypotension. Name it in your report, because the hospital treatment is replacement steroids.

quiz.q: A 74-year-old woman with chest pain takes a medication labeled Revatio. What does this mean for your care?
choices: It is a diuretic and is irrelevant to nitroglycerin
It only matters in male patients
It is sildenafil for pulmonary hypertension and contraindicates nitroglycerin for 24 hours
It is a nitrate, so she may take additional nitroglycerin safely
quiz.why: Revatio is sildenafil dosed for pulmonary hypertension, and the nitrate interaction is identical regardless of why it was prescribed or the patient's sex. Ask about medications for circulation and the lungs, not only about erectile dysfunction.

quiz.q: Which counter of medications most strongly suggests a patient with severe COPD?
choices: Tiotropium, monthly albuterol refills, a prednisone taper, and home oxygen
Levothyroxine, allopurinol, and omeprazole
Apixaban, diltiazem, and digoxin
Carbidopa-levodopa and donepezil
quiz.why: That combination describes advanced obstructive lung disease, which also tells you to titrate oxygen to 88 to 92 percent and expect a high baseline carbon dioxide. The other sets describe atrial fibrillation and neurologic disease.

quiz.q: You find a bottle of 60 furosemide tablets filled 55 days ago with 48 remaining in a patient with severe leg swelling and orthopnea. What is the most useful conclusion?
choices: The dose is too low and should be doubled
The bottle is nearly new and tells you nothing
The medication has expired
He has taken roughly 12 of 55 expected doses, so nonadherence likely explains the fluid overload
quiz.why: Counting tablets against the fill date converts a bottle into adherence data. Twelve doses in fifty-five days explains the volume overload better than any new diagnosis, and it belongs in your report.

quiz.q: A child weighs 44 lb. Your protocol calls for 0.01 mg/kg of epinephrine from a 1 mg/mL vial. What dose and volume are correct?
choices: 0.44 mg, which is 0.44 mL
0.1 mg, which is 0.1 mL
0.2 mg, which is 0.2 mL
2 mg, which is 2 mL
quiz.why: 44 divided by 2.2 is 20 kg; 20 times 0.01 mg/kg is 0.2 mg; 0.2 divided by 1 mg/mL is 0.2 mL. Working the conversion first is what prevents a tenfold error.

quiz.q: An E cylinder reads 1,000 psi and you are running a nonrebreather at 15 L/min. Approximately how many minutes of oxygen remain?
choices: About 15 minutes
About 19 minutes
About 28 minutes
About 40 minutes
quiz.why: 1,000 minus the 200 psi safe residual is 800; times the E constant of 0.28 is 224; divided by 15 L/min is about 15 minutes. Forgetting the residual overestimates your supply.

quiz.q: You are handed a vial labeled epinephrine 0.1 mg/mL and asked for an adult intramuscular anaphylaxis dose. What is the correct response?
choices: Draw 0.3 mL and give it intramuscularly
Draw 3 mL and give it intravenously
Draw 0.03 mL and give it intramuscularly
Recognize this is the cardiac arrest concentration, obtain the 1 mg/mL vial, and give 0.3 mL intramuscularly
quiz.why: 0.3 mg from a 0.1 mg/mL vial would require 3 mL, which is not an IM anaphylaxis product, and 0.3 mL of it delivers only 0.03 mg. Reading the concentration every single time is the safeguard.

quiz.q: Medical direction orders 25 g of dextrose. Which of the following delivers exactly that?
choices: 100 mL of D50
50 mL of D50 or 250 mL of D10
25 mL of D10
500 mL of D50
quiz.why: A percent solution is grams per 100 mL, so D50 is 0.5 g/mL and 50 mL contains 25 g, while D10 is 0.1 g/mL and requires 250 mL for the same 25 g.

quiz.q: You must give 2 mg of naloxone intramuscularly from a vial labeled 0.4 mg/mL. What volume do you draw?
choices: 0.8 mL
2 mL
5 mL
0.5 mL
quiz.why: Volume equals dose divided by concentration: 2 divided by 0.4 equals 5 mL. The weaker the solution, the larger the volume for the same dose.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old with a history of myocardial infarction is in anaphylaxis with stridor and a BP of 86/50. What is the correct epinephrine decision?
choices: Give the standard 0.3 mg intramuscularly in the thigh and monitor closely
Give a reduced dose of 0.15 mg because of his cardiac history
Withhold epinephrine and give oxygen only
Give epinephrine subcutaneously to slow absorption
quiz.why: Cardiac disease and age are cautions, not contraindications; untreated anaphylaxis kills far more reliably than IM epinephrine harms. Reducing the dose on your own or switching routes delays the only drug that reverses all three problems at once.

quiz.q: An 8 kg infant has anaphylaxis after a milk exposure. Your kit holds 0.15 mg and 0.3 mg auto-injectors and, under protocol, a 1 mg/mL vial with syringes. What is best?
choices: The 0.15 mg auto-injector
The 0.3 mg auto-injector
Withhold epinephrine and transport
Draw up 0.01 mg/kg, which is 0.08 mg, or 0.08 mL of the 1 mg/mL concentration
quiz.why: Below about 7.5 to 15 kg the auto-injector needle is too long and the fixed dose is too large, so the calculated dose drawn from a vial is correct where protocol allows it. Withholding epinephrine in anaphylaxis is never the answer.

quiz.q: Ten minutes after 0.3 mg of epinephrine, a patient on propranolol still has wheezing and a systolic of 82. What should you do and what should you tell the hospital?
choices: Withhold further epinephrine and transport quietly
Repeat the epinephrine per protocol and report the beta blocker so glucagon can be considered
Give a double dose of epinephrine to overcome the blockade
Switch to an antihistamine as the primary treatment
quiz.why: Beta blockade blunts the response, making a repeat dose more likely to be needed. Doubling on your own is not the protocol answer; the hospital's tool for refractory beta-blocked anaphylaxis is glucagon 1 to 5 mg IV.

quiz.q: While injecting a struggling 4-year-old, the auto-injector fires into your thumb. What should you do?
choices: Nothing; the dose is too small to matter
Apply ice to the digit to reduce swelling
Keep the hand warm, note the time, and get the digit evaluated at an emergency department
Inject the remaining dose into the thumb from the other side
quiz.why: Epinephrine constricts the small vessels of a digit, producing a white, cold, numb finger that can be injured by prolonged ischemia. Warmth helps; ice makes vasoconstriction worse.

quiz.q: A hospice patient on high-dose morphine for cancer pain is breathing 5 times a minute. What is the safest approach?
choices: Give 4 mg intranasal naloxone immediately and repeat every minute
Withhold all treatment because he is a hospice patient
Give naloxone only after 10 minutes of ventilation
