Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and use the smallest effective naloxone dose, titrated to adequate breathing
quiz.why: Ventilation addresses the lethal problem immediately. Full reversal in an opioid-dependent patient causes severe withdrawal and uncontrolled pain, so titrate to about 12 breaths a minute with good chest rise rather than to alertness. Goals of care should also be clarified with medical direction.

quiz.q: You are bagging a suspected fentanyl overdose and the chest feels extremely stiff with almost no air movement despite a good seal and an airway adjunct. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Fentanyl-induced chest wall rigidity, which naloxone reverses
A tension pneumothorax
Complete foreign body obstruction
The bag-valve mask is broken
quiz.why: High-potency opioids can stiffen chest and abdominal muscles so that ventilation feels obstructed. Continue two-person ventilation and give naloxone, which reverses the rigidity; assuming obstruction leads to the wrong interventions.

quiz.q: A patient reversed with naloxone is now awake, vomiting, furious, and demanding to be left alone at the scene. What is the most accurate framing and the correct action?
choices: He is being hostile and should be restrained
He is now fine and can be released without further discussion
This is precipitated withdrawal; protect the airway, de-escalate, involve medical direction, and strongly encourage transport because re-sedation is likely
Give a second naloxone dose to keep him awake longer
quiz.why: Agitation and vomiting after naloxone are withdrawal, not character. Naloxone lasts 30 to 90 minutes while most opioids last longer, so refusal carries a real risk of arrest after you leave. Document the capacity assessment and the risks explained.

quiz.q: A newborn delivered to a mother with opioid use disorder is limp and apneic at 30 seconds of life. What is the correct treatment?
choices: Intranasal naloxone at half the adult dose
Warm, dry, stimulate, position and ventilate at 40 to 60 breaths per minute; naloxone is not used
Naloxone 0.1 mg/kg intramuscularly, then ventilate
Chest compressions immediately
quiz.why: Naloxone is not part of neonatal resuscitation and may precipitate seizures in an exposed newborn. Effective ventilation corrects nearly all newborn depression, and compressions wait for a heart rate under 60 after 30 seconds of good ventilation.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old with crushing substernal pain takes warfarin for a mechanical heart valve. What should you do about aspirin?
choices: Give 324 mg chewed per protocol and report the warfarin clearly at the hospital
Withhold aspirin because he is anticoagulated
Give 81 mg as a compromise dose
Give aspirin only if he has not taken warfarin today
quiz.why: Aspirin and warfarin act on different parts of clotting, and most protocols still give the full dose for suspected ACS because the benefit in a growing coronary clot is large. The hospital needs the anticoagulant named for its own decisions.

quiz.q: A patient with chest pain has asthma, nasal polyps, and a history of severe wheezing after taking ibuprofen. What is the correct decision about aspirin?
choices: Give the full 324 mg, since polyps are unrelated
Give aspirin and have an inhaler ready
Withhold aspirin, because this pattern is aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, and document why
Give a single 81 mg tablet to test tolerance
quiz.why: Asthma plus nasal polyps plus prior wheezing after aspirin or an NSAID is a real contraindication, not an intolerance. Test doses are never appropriate, and the withheld medication plus the reason belongs in the chart.

quiz.q: You are about to defibrillate a cardiac arrest patient and notice a nitroglycerin patch on the left upper chest. What should you do?
choices: Defibrillate through it to avoid delay
Leave it because the medication may help
Place the pads directly over the patch for better contact
Remove the patch with a gloved hand, wipe the skin, and then place the pads
quiz.why: The metallic backing of a patch can arc and burn the skin during defibrillation, and the patch continues delivering a vasodilator. Removal takes seconds and belongs in the same motion as exposing the chest.

quiz.q: A patient with chest pain has taken three of his own nitroglycerin tablets with no relief. The bottle was opened 14 months ago and rides in his truck. BP is 128/78. What is the most useful conclusion?
choices: The pain is definitely not cardiac, since nitroglycerin did not help
The tablets may be inert from age, heat and light, so lack of relief does not rule out a cardiac cause
He should take three more of the same tablets
Burning under the tongue would have proven the tablets were good
quiz.why: Sublingual tablets degrade within about 3 to 6 months of opening, faster in heat. Failure to relieve pain with a possibly inert supply proves nothing, and the burning sensation is not a reliable potency test.

quiz.q: A diabetic is unresponsive with a glucose of 31 mg/dL and no gag reflex. Your service carries glucagon. What do you do?
choices: Place oral glucose gel between the cheek and gum
Manage the airway, give glucagon 1 mg IM, position on the side anticipating vomiting, and request ALS
Wait for ALS without treating
Give glucagon and oral glucose together for a faster effect
quiz.why: Buccal absorption in an unresponsive patient is negligible and risks aspiration. Glucagon works without swallowing, takes 8 to 15 minutes, and commonly causes vomiting, so airway control and positioning travel with it.

quiz.q: Twenty minutes after intramuscular glucagon, a patient with a long history of alcohol use and liver disease is still unresponsive with a glucose of 36 mg/dL. What is the best explanation?
choices: His liver has little stored glycogen for glucagon to mobilize, so he needs intravenous dextrose
The glucagon was given in the wrong muscle
Glucagon takes at least an hour to work
Glucagon does not work in type 2 diabetes
quiz.why: Glucagon releases stored liver glycogen; chronic alcohol use, starvation and liver disease deplete those stores. Dextrose supplies the sugar directly and is the required treatment.

quiz.q: A sweaty, confused patient wearing a continuous glucose sensor shows a sensor reading of 96 mg/dL. What should you do?
choices: Accept the reading and look for another cause
Remove the sensor and reapply it
Confirm with a fingerstick, because sensors lag capillary glucose by 5 to 15 minutes and read high during a rapid fall
Give oral glucose without any measurement
quiz.why: Sensors measure interstitial fluid, which trails blood glucose. During a fast drop the sensor can look normal while the patient is profoundly hypoglycemic. Treat the patient and verify with a fingerstick.

quiz.q: A student asks whether an EMT can administer glucagon. What is the most accurate answer?
choices: Yes, everywhere, because it is in the national scope
No, it is always an ALS medication
Only physicians may authorize it in an emergency
It depends on state regulation, your medical director's protocol, and your own credential
quiz.why: The national scope model is a floor; states, the agency medical director and individual credentialing all have to align. That is why the honest answer is always framed as 'per protocol' and documented with the authorizing standing order.

quiz.q: A patient in pulmonary edema has been on CPAP at 10 cm H2O for seven minutes. He is now harder to rouse and his systolic has dropped from 172 to 94. What should you do?
choices: Increase pressure to 15 cm H2O
Remove CPAP and ventilate with a bag-valve mask while treating the hypotension
Tighten the straps to fix the seal
Continue and reassess in another ten minutes
quiz.why: Declining mental status and hypotension are both CPAP failure criteria, and positive pressure reduces venous return. A patient who can no longer cooperate or protect the airway needs assisted ventilation instead.

quiz.q: When is a CPAP patient most likely to deteriorate suddenly?
choices: When the mask is removed during a transfer to the hospital bed
During the first 30 seconds of application
While the pressure is being titrated from 5 to 10 cm H2O
When oxygen is blended into the circuit
quiz.why: The pressure is doing continuous work, so taking it off even briefly allows air sacs to collapse and fluid to return. Keep it on through hallway moves and the bed transfer until the receiving team is ready.

quiz.q: Midway through transport you realize you gave a 24 kg child the 0.3 mg adult auto-injector instead of the 0.15 mg pediatric device. What is your first priority?
choices: Notify your supervisor by radio
Complete the quality-assurance form before arrival
Reassess the patient and take a full set of vitals, monitoring for tachycardia, hypertension and chest discomfort
Amend the chart to reflect the correct dose
quiz.why: The patient comes first. Notification, explicit disclosure at handoff, objective documentation and the incident report all follow immediately after, and altering a chart to hide the dose would be far more serious than the error itself.

quiz.q: An experienced EMT with a clean record grabs the wrong strength auto-injector during a chaotic scene and reports it immediately. Under just culture, what is the appropriate organizational response?
choices: Suspension, because patient safety allows no exceptions
Termination if any harm occurred
No response at all, so reporting is not discouraged
Treat it as human error: support the provider and fix the system that allowed two strengths to be confused
quiz.why: Just culture separates human error, at-risk behavior and recklessness. Punishing slips suppresses reporting and destroys the data that prevents repeats; the durable fix is packaging, labeling and a two-person check.

quiz.q: You discover that you charted the wrong administration time for a nitroglycerin dose after the report was submitted electronically. What is the correct correction?
choices: Add a timestamped addendum stating the correct time and the reason for the correction
Ask a supervisor to delete the original entry
Leave the error, since the time is a minor detail
Overwrite the original field so the record reads correctly
quiz.why: A medical record must preserve what was originally documented. An addendum with its own timestamp corrects the information transparently; deleting or overwriting looks like concealment and creates a much larger problem.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 68M, chest pressure, 'he takes a lot of pills'
scenarios.intro: 1510 hours. Ranch house, patient seated at the kitchen table. Dispatch: 68-year-old male, chest pressure for 40 minutes. His wife has gathered eight pill bottles on the table: aspirin 81 mg, apixaban, metoprolol, atorvastatin, furosemide, tamsulosin, nitroglycerin, and one labeled Adcirca. He took his usual morning medications. ALS is 7 minutes out; the hospital is 18 minutes away.

steps.prompt: He describes pressure across the middle of his chest with an ache in his left jaw that started while he was moving boxes. He is pale, mildly diaphoretic, and rates it 7 out of 10. His wife says he took his 81 mg aspirin at 7 a.m. as always.

choices.text: Give 324 mg of chewable aspirin now, chewed, and request ALS
choices.feedback: Correct. Daily low-dose aspirin does not provide the acute platelet blockade needed, so the full 324 mg is still indicated. The apixaban does not change that in most protocols.

choices.text: Withhold aspirin because he is on apixaban and already took 81 mg
choices.feedback: Wrong on both counts. Anticoagulants work on a different part of clotting, and a daily 81 mg dose is not an acute dose.

choices.text: Apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min before anything else
choices.feedback: Not indicated. His saturation is 96 percent. Routine high-flow oxygen for every chest pain has not been the standard for years.

choices.text: Obtain a full set of vitals and a SAMPLE history first, then give aspirin
choices.feedback: Acceptable but slower. Aspirin is time-critical in a growing coronary clot and can be given while the history continues.

steps.prompt: His wife holds up his nitroglycerin and asks if he should take one. You ask about medications for circulation, the lungs, or erections in the last two days. He says the Adcirca is 'for the pressure in my lungs' and he took one about 30 hours ago.

choices.text: Withhold nitroglycerin: Adcirca is tadalafil, and the interval is 48 hours, not 24
choices.feedback: Correct. Tadalafil is the long one. Thirty hours is well inside the 48-hour window, and combining them can cause an unrecoverable drop in pressure.

choices.text: Assist with one 0.4 mg dose since more than 24 hours have passed
choices.feedback: Dangerous. The 24-hour rule belongs to sildenafil and vardenafil. Tadalafil requires 48 hours.

choices.text: Assist with nitroglycerin because his blood pressure is adequate
choices.feedback: The pressure is only one of the two checks. The PDE-5 question is the other, and it fails here.

choices.text: Contact medical direction, describe the tadalafil timing, and follow their order
choices.feedback: Reasonable and safe. Even so, know the answer yourself: 48 hours for tadalafil.

steps.prompt: Ten minutes into transport his pain rises to 9 out of 10, he becomes gray and clammy, and he says he feels like he is going to pass out.

choices.text: Lay him flat, elevate the legs, start oxygen to bring saturation to 94 percent or higher, and expedite the ALS intercept
choices.feedback: Correct. He is hypotensive and now hypoxic, so oxygen is indicated where it was not before. Position supports preload while ALS brings fluid and monitoring.

choices.text: Assist with nitroglycerin now that the pain has worsened
choices.feedback: Harmful twice over: the tadalafil window is still open and he is already hypotensive.

choices.text: Sit him fully upright so he can breathe more easily
choices.feedback: Wrong direction with a systolic of 92 and presyncope. Upright reduces cerebral and coronary perfusion.

choices.text: Give a second dose of aspirin to strengthen the effect
choices.feedback: No. The 324 mg dose is complete; more aspirin adds bleeding risk and no benefit.

steps.prompt: You notice his heart rate has stayed between 78 and 84 through all of this, even as his pressure fell and his skin turned gray.

choices.text: Recognize that metoprolol is preventing the expected tachycardia, and judge perfusion by skin, mental status and capillary refill
choices.feedback: Correct. A beta blocker removes the heart rate as a witness. The gray skin and the falling pressure are the real data.

choices.text: Take the stable heart rate as evidence he is compensating well
choices.feedback: This is the trap the drug sets. A normal rate on a beta blocker proves nothing about perfusion.

choices.text: Conclude the blood pressure cuff is malfunctioning because the rate has not changed
choices.feedback: Rechecking a pressure is fine, but do not explain away a consistent finding that matches the patient's appearance.

steps.prompt: The paramedic steps in for the intercept and asks for your report.

choices.text: Chest pain with radiation, aspirin 324 mg chewed at 1516, nitroglycerin withheld because of tadalafil about 30 hours ago, metoprolol blunting the heart rate, and the pressure trend with times
choices.feedback: Correct. The withheld drug and the reason are as important as what you gave, and the beta blocker changes how everyone reads the vital signs.

choices.text: Report the vitals and that you gave aspirin
choices.feedback: Incomplete. Without the tadalafil, the next provider may reach for nitroglycerin, and without the beta blocker the heart rate will be misread.

choices.text: Say the patient refused nitroglycerin
choices.feedback: Inaccurate. You withheld it for a contraindication, and the chart must say so. Misstating it puts the patient at risk and misrepresents your care.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: the medication list runs this call. Daily low-dose aspirin never blocks the acute 324 mg dose, and anticoagulation does not either. Tadalafil, sold as Cialis or Adcirca, requires 48 hours before nitroglycerin, not 24, and it is prescribed to men and women for pulmonary hypertension. A beta blocker holds the heart rate steady while the patient deteriorates, so read skin, mental status and pressure instead. Finally, a withheld medication with its reason is a documented treatment decision, not an omission.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 9-year-old diabetic, 'we can't wake her up'
scenarios.intro: 0620 hours. Dispatch: 9-year-old female, type 1 diabetic, unresponsive in bed. Father says she went to bed without finishing dinner after soccer practice and had a stomach bug yesterday. She wears an insulin pump on her waistband and a sensor patch on her arm. She weighs about 62 lb. Your protocol authorizes glucagon. ALS is 12 minutes out.

steps.prompt: She is limp and unresponsive to voice, with snoring respirations and a thread of saliva at the corner of her mouth. Her skin is cool and drenched in sweat. Her father is holding a tube of glucose gel and asks if he should put it in her mouth.

choices.text: Stop him, open the airway with a jaw thrust or head tilt, suction as needed, give oxygen, and check a glucose
choices.feedback: Correct. Nothing goes in the mouth of a patient who cannot protect the airway, and the snoring is an airway you can fix in five seconds.

choices.text: Let him place the gel between the cheek and gum since buccal absorption is safe
choices.feedback: Wrong and dangerous. Buccal absorption is negligible and she will aspirate it. This is a common piece of outdated teaching.

choices.text: Move straight to glucagon before assessing the airway
choices.feedback: Out of order. Glucagon takes 8 to 15 minutes; the airway takes seconds and is what is threatening her right now.

choices.text: Trust the sensor on her arm, which reads 104 mg/dL, and look for another cause
choices.feedback: Trap. Sensors lag blood by 5 to 15 minutes and read high during a fast fall. Confirm with a fingerstick.

steps.prompt: The fingerstick reads 28 mg/dL. The airway is clear with an oral airway in place and she tolerates it. The pump is still running and the small screen shows an active basal rate.

choices.text: Ask the father to suspend or disconnect the pump, and note the time it was stopped
choices.feedback: Correct. The pump keeps delivering insulin straight through a low unless somebody stops it, and the father knows the device far better than you do.

choices.text: Start pressing buttons on the pump yourself to stop it
choices.feedback: Risky. Unfamiliar hardware in a crisis is how a bolus gets delivered by accident. Ask the person who uses it daily.

choices.text: Cut the infusion set tubing immediately
choices.feedback: Unnecessary and outside most protocols. Suspending or disconnecting at the site is cleaner and reversible.

choices.text: Leave the pump alone because stopping it may cause high sugar later
choices.feedback: Wrong priority. Hypoglycemia is killing brain cells now; a temporary rise later is a hospital problem.

steps.prompt: She weighs 62 lb. Your protocol authorizes glucagon 1 mg intramuscularly for patients about 25 kg and above, and 0.5 mg below that. The kit is the powder vial with a diluent syringe.

choices.text: Convert 62 lb to about 28 kg, reconstitute the vial by injecting the diluent and swirling until clear, give 1 mg IM in the thigh, and position her on her side
choices.feedback: Correct on all four counts. She is above the 25 kg cutoff, the kit must be reconstituted before use, and vomiting is the expected side effect.

choices.text: Give 0.5 mg because she is a child
choices.feedback: Under-dosed. The cutoff is weight, not age, and 62 lb is about 28 kg.

choices.text: Inject the powder without the diluent to save time
choices.feedback: Not possible. The powder must be dissolved in the supplied diluent; this is exactly why practicing with a training kit matters.

choices.text: Give the 1 mg dose but leave her supine to monitor the airway more easily
choices.feedback: Half right. The dose is correct, but vomiting after glucagon is common and a supine, obtunded patient will aspirate. Side-lying with suction ready.

steps.prompt: Twelve minutes later she vomits once, then opens her eyes and is confused but answering. Repeat glucose is 74 mg/dL. Her father says she seems fine now and asks whether she can just stay home and eat breakfast.

choices.text: Explain that she needs transport: the pump was suspended, she has been vomiting, and the low can return; recheck glucose before arrival
choices.feedback: Correct. An unresolved cause plus an interrupted insulin plan plus vomiting is not a refusal candidate, and glucagon buys time rather than fixing anything.

choices.text: Agree to leave her home if she eats a candy bar
choices.feedback: Unsafe. Simple sugar alone leads to a second drop, the underlying cause is unaddressed, and her pump is off.

choices.text: Let her father decide without further discussion, since she is awake
choices.feedback: You owe the family the risks in plain language, and medical direction should be involved in any refusal after a severe hypoglycemic episode.

choices.text: Offer a sandwich with protein if she can swallow safely, while continuing to transport
choices.feedback: Good. Once she is fully awake and protecting her airway, complex carbohydrate with protein prevents the rebound low. Transport continues.

steps.prompt: You arrive at the pediatric emergency department. The nurse asks what happened.

choices.text: Give the timeline with numbers: glucose 28 at 0626, glucagon 1 mg IM right thigh at 0634, pump suspended by father at 0631, vomited once at 0646, glucose 74 at 0648, and her level of consciousness at each point
choices.feedback: Correct. Glucose values with times, the dose and site, and the pump status are exactly what the receiving team needs to decide about dextrose and admission.

choices.text: Report that she was hypoglycemic, got glucagon, and is better now
choices.feedback: Too thin. Without the numbers and times the hospital cannot judge her trajectory or predict a second low.

choices.text: Report the sensor reading of 104 as the presenting glucose
choices.feedback: Inaccurate and misleading. The fingerstick was 28; the sensor was lagging. Report measured values with their source.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: hypoglycemia in a patient who cannot swallow is an airway call first and a sugar call second. Nothing goes in the mouth, sensors lag and must be confirmed with a fingerstick, and an insulin pump keeps working through the emergency until the person who owns it stops it. Glucagon is weight-based at about 25 kg, needs reconstitution, takes 8 to 15 minutes, and reliably causes vomiting, so position for it. A patient who wakes up is not a patient who is fixed: document glucose values with times, and transport when the cause is unresolved.

scenarios.title: The wrong auto-injector
scenarios.intro: 1750 hours. You are transporting a 22 kg seven-year-old with anaphylaxis after eating a cookie containing walnuts. Your partner drew the auto-injector from the pediatric pouch and gave it in the left thigh while you managed the airway and oxygen. Four minutes later, cleaning up, you see the spent device on the bench: it is the 0.3 mg adult unit. The child weighs 22 kg, which calls for 0.15 mg. You are nine minutes from the hospital.

steps.prompt: You are certain about what you are looking at. Your partner is at the head of the stretcher and has not noticed. The child's hives are fading and her stridor has resolved.

choices.text: Say it out loud to your partner immediately, then reassess the patient fully and take a complete set of vitals
choices.feedback: Correct. Patient first, honesty immediately. A doubled dose needs monitoring for tachycardia, hypertension and chest discomfort, and your partner is part of that monitoring.

choices.text: Say nothing for now and decide after you see how she does
choices.feedback: This is where an error becomes harm. Concealment removes the second set of eyes and delays the receiving team's preparation.

choices.text: Quietly dispose of the device so it is not confusing at the hospital
choices.feedback: Never. That is tampering with evidence of care, and the spent device is part of the record. This crosses from error into reckless behavior.

choices.text: Start filling out the incident form right now
choices.feedback: Out of order. Paperwork is important and comes after the patient is reassessed and the team is informed.

steps.prompt: Your partner is visibly shaken and starts apologizing. The child is alert, shaky, and says her heart feels 'fast and funny.' Her mother is sitting beside her and heard the conversation.

choices.text: Tell the mother plainly what happened and what it means, keep monitoring, and reassure the child that the fast heartbeat is expected from the medication
choices.feedback: Correct. Plain, non-defensive disclosure to the family is the standard, and it is easier now than after they hear it at the hospital.

choices.text: Tell the mother the fast heart rate is from the allergic reaction
choices.feedback: False. The reaction is resolving and the tachycardia is from the double dose. A false explanation is far more damaging than the error.

choices.text: Focus on blaming the pouch labeling in front of the family
choices.feedback: The labeling probably is a real system problem, and it belongs in the quality-assurance report, not in a conversation at the patient's bedside.

choices.text: Say nothing to the mother and let the hospital explain it
choices.feedback: Avoidable damage. The family will learn it anyway, and hearing it first from you is what preserves trust.

steps.prompt: Two minutes out. The child's heart rate is settling slightly and she denies chest pain. You are about to give your handoff.

choices.text: State it explicitly in the verbal report: 22 kg child, 0.3 mg epinephrine IM left thigh at 1746 instead of the intended 0.15 mg, with vitals since
choices.feedback: Correct. Say it out loud in the handoff. Burying it in the written chart and hoping someone reads it is not disclosure.

choices.text: Write it in the chart and let them read it there
choices.feedback: Insufficient. A verbal handoff is what shapes the next hour of care, and a doubled dose changes their monitoring plan.

choices.text: Report the dose given without mentioning the intended dose
choices.feedback: Half a disclosure. Stating both the given and intended doses is what makes the error usable information for the team.

steps.prompt: At the station, you sit down with the report. Your partner asks whether you can 'just put 0.15 since that's what the protocol says' because the child is fine.

choices.text: Refuse: document the drug, dose, route, site, time, the patient's response, and who you notified, as facts without blame
choices.feedback: Correct. Falsifying a chart is reckless behavior and a far more serious matter than the original slip, which was a human error.

choices.text: Agree, since no harm came to the patient
choices.feedback: This turns a survivable mistake into misconduct. Outcome does not change what was actually given.

choices.text: Leave the dose field blank so nobody has to decide
choices.feedback: An omission in a medication record is its own error and looks worse later than an honest entry does.

choices.text: Write the facts and add a narrative line about the two strengths being stored in the same pouch
choices.feedback: Good. Objective description of the conditions helps the review find the system fix, as long as it stays factual and not accusatory.

steps.prompt: Your supervisor asks you both to walk through it. Your partner is worried about being disciplined.

choices.text: Describe it as a human error under just culture, file the quality-assurance report, and propose separating the two strengths and adding a two-person check for pediatric doses
choices.feedback: Correct. Human error gets support and a system fix; the durable prevention is packaging and a verbal double-check, not a lecture.

choices.text: Argue that no report is needed because the patient was unharmed
choices.feedback: Near-misses and no-harm events are the cheapest safety data available. Not reporting removes the only chance to fix the pouch.

choices.text: Accept that your partner should be suspended to make the point
choices.feedback: Punishing a slip drives reporting underground and guarantees the next crew repeats it. Discipline is reserved for reckless behavior.

choices.text: Ask about peer support or the employee assistance program for both of you
choices.feedback: Worth doing. Clinicians who harm a patient by accident predictably struggle afterward, and agencies maintain these programs for exactly this.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: the five minutes after an error decide everything. Reassess and treat the patient, say it out loud to your partner, tell the family plainly, and state it explicitly in the verbal handoff rather than burying it in the chart. Document facts without blame and never alter a record, because falsification is reckless behavior while the original slip was human error. Then push the fix upstream: two strengths in one pouch is a system problem, and a two-person check on weight-based pediatric doses is what stops it happening to the next crew.
